\begin{abstract}
We isolate the minimal combinatorial structure underlying unique-decomposition
theorems. A \emph{quotient system} is a labelled step relation on a class of
objects, equipped with a natural-number rank, subject to exactly three axioms:
every step strictly decreases rank (\emph{termination}), the label of a step is
determined by its endpoints (\emph{label determinacy}), and two distinct steps
out of a common source close into a diamond with labels exchanged
(\emph{exchange}, an abstract Zassenhaus/butterfly axiom). A \emph{quotient
step} is one such move; an \emph{evolutionary path} is a finite chain of them,
recording the list of labels used, and is \emph{complete} when it ends at a
terminal object admitting no further step.

Our main theorem---an abstract Jordan--H\"older theorem---states that any two
complete evolutionary paths out of the same object end at the same terminal
object and use the same multiset of labels. This produces a well-defined
multiset-valued invariant $\dcmp(x)$ satisfying a one-step law, a terminality
criterion, and a conservation law asserting that the labels of an arbitrary path
equal the multiset difference of the invariants at its endpoints. As structural
corollaries, reachability is an antisymmetric, graded, confluent preorder, and
the invariant is functorial for step-preserving maps.

We show the three axioms are independent: for each, an explicit finite
counterexample satisfying the other two invalidates the corresponding
conclusion. We prove a universality theorem---every quotient system maps to the
system of multisets under deletion---and determine exactly when that
representation is faithful: the naive conjecture fails on a four-element
diamond, but holds under a \emph{separation} hypothesis, via a pull-forward
(commutation) lemma. Adding a \emph{saturation} hypothesis yields a complete
classification: the stages reachable from $x$ are in bijection with the
sub-multisets of $\dcmp(x)$, and the label lists of complete paths out of $x$
are exactly the permutations of $\dcmp(x)$.

Two instantiations are developed. In the multiplicative monoid of natural
numbers, with steps dividing out a prime, the abstract theorem specialises to
the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, the invariant is the prime factorisation,
its cardinality is $\Omega$, its label multiplicities are the $p$-adic
valuations, reachability is divisibility, and the classification theorem is the
divisor--sub-multiset correspondence. On finite sets, with steps deleting one
element, the invariant is the underlying multiset; the prime-product map bridges
the two instances and yields squarefreeness and injectivity results without
multiplicative computation. Finally, weighting labels produces \emph{path
weights} and \emph{path actions}, conserved potentials of the flow, and
characterises the completely multiplicative and completely additive arithmetic
functions as exactly the path weights and path actions of their own restrictions
to the prime labels.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The recurring phenomenon}

Across mathematics one meets the same statement in different dialects.

\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Fundamental theorem of arithmetic.} Every positive integer factors
      into primes, uniquely up to order.
\item \emph{Jordan--H\"older theorem.} Every composition series of a finite
      group has the same length and the same multiset of simple factors.
\item \emph{Deletion in finite sets.} Removing the elements of a finite set one
      at a time takes exactly $|S|$ steps and uses each element once.
\item \emph{Normal forms in rewriting.} A terminating, confluent rewriting
      system assigns a unique normal form to each term.
\end{itemize}

Each is proved separately in its own subject, with its own machinery. The
question this paper answers is: what is the common core? Specifically, what is
the weakest hypothesis set on an abstract ``breaking apart'' process under which
the conclusion ``the decomposition is independent of every choice'' is a
theorem?

\subsection{Method: define the vocabulary before the conjecture}

The methodological commitment of this work is to define the two operative
notions---\emph{quotient step} and \emph{evolutionary path}---with full
precision \emph{before} attempting the decomposition conjecture. This is not
pedantry. Once the notion of a step is fixed to the three axioms below, the
decomposition conjecture becomes a decidable question about that axiom set, and,
crucially, the \emph{sharpness} of the answer becomes testable: we can and do
ask, for each axiom, whether it may be dropped.

\subsection{Summary of contributions}

Definitions (\S\ref{sec:defs}); the decomposition theorem and its invariant
(\S\ref{sec:decomp}); independence of the three axioms (\S\ref{sec:sharp});
the arithmetic and combinatorial instances with a bridge between them
(\S\ref{sec:inst}); universality of multiset deletion, failure and repair of
faithfulness (\S\ref{sec:univ}); classification of futures under saturation
(\S\ref{sec:class}); path weights, path actions and arithmetic functions
(\S\ref{sec:integral}); algorithms (\S\ref{sec:algo}); discussion and open
problems (\S\ref{sec:disc}--\S\ref{sec:open}).

\section{Definitions}\label{sec:defs}

Throughout, $\alpha$ denotes a class of \emph{objects} and $\Lambda$ a class of
\emph{labels}.

\begin{definition}[Quotient system]\label{def:qs}
A \emph{quotient system} $Q$ on $(\alpha, \Lambda)$ consists of a ternary
relation $\mathrm{step}_Q \subseteq \alpha \times \Lambda \times \alpha$,
written $x \step{\ell} y$ and read ``$y$ is obtained from $x$ by a quotient step
of type $\ell$'', together with a \emph{rank} function
$\rk_Q : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$, satisfying:
\begin{description}
\item[(A1) Termination.] If $x \step{\ell} y$ then $\rk_Q(y) < \rk_Q(x)$.
\item[(A2) Label determinacy.] If $x \step{\ell_1} y$ and $x \step{\ell_2} y$
      then $\ell_1 = \ell_2$.
\item[(A3) Exchange.] If $x \step{\ell_1} y_1$ and $x \step{\ell_2} y_2$ with
      $y_1 \neq y_2$, then there is $z$ with $y_1 \step{\ell_2} z$ and
      $y_2 \step{\ell_1} z$.
\end{description}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Quotient step]
A \emph{quotient step} is an instance of $\mathrm{step}_Q$: a triple
$(x,\ell,y)$ with $x \step{\ell} y$. It is the atomic move of the theory: one
labelled, rank-decreasing, exchange-closed reduction.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}
(A1) is termination in the sense of rewriting theory: it forbids infinite
evolution and supplies the induction measure for every proof below. (A2) says
the ``isomorphism type of the quotient'' is well defined: knowing where you
started and where you landed determines what you divided out. (A3) is the
abstract form of the Zassenhaus butterfly lemma and simultaneously a labelled
local-confluence condition. Note that (A3) is silent when $y_1 = y_2$, which is
exactly the case handled by (A2). Nothing else is assumed; in particular a given
source $x$ and label $\ell$ may admit several targets.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Evolutionary path]
For $x,t \in \alpha$ and a list $L = [\ell_1,\dots,\ell_k]$ of labels, an
\emph{evolutionary path} from $x$ to $t$ with label list $L$ is a finite chain
\[ x = x_0 \step{\ell_1} x_1 \step{\ell_2} \cdots \step{\ell_k} x_k = t. \]
Formally the relation is generated by the empty path from $x$ to $x$ with label
list $[\,]$, and by prefixing a quotient step $x \step{\ell} y$ to a path from
$y$ to $t$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Terminal, complete, reachable]
An object $t$ is \emph{terminal} if no quotient step leaves it. An evolutionary
path is \emph{complete} if its endpoint is terminal. We write $x \reach y$ (``$y$
is reachable from $x$'', or ``$y$ is a \emph{stage in the future of} $x$'') if
some evolutionary path runs from $x$ to $y$.
\end{definition}

Immediate consequences of (A1): rank is nonincreasing along a path, and the
length of any path out of $x$ is at most $\rk_Q(x)$. Paths concatenate, the
label lists concatenating with them.

\begin{proposition}[Termination of evolution]\label{prop:exists}
Every object $x$ admits a complete evolutionary path.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Strong induction on $\rk_Q(x)$. If $x$ is terminal, the empty path suffices.
Otherwise choose any step $x \step{\ell} y$; by (A1) $\rk_Q(y) < \rk_Q(x)$, so by
induction $y$ admits a complete path, and prefixing the step gives one for $x$.
\end{proof}

\section{The Decomposition Theorem}\label{sec:decomp}

Write $\ms{L}$ for the multiset underlying a list $L$, and $\uplus$ for multiset
union.

\begin{theorem}[Abstract Jordan--H\"older / Decomposition Theorem]\label{thm:jh}
Let $Q$ be a quotient system. Suppose there are complete evolutionary paths out
of $x$, one ending at $t_1$ with label list $L_1$ and one ending at $t_2$ with
label list $L_2$. Then $t_1 = t_2$ and $\ms{L_1} = \ms{L_2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Strong induction on $n = \rk_Q(x)$.

If either path is empty, its source is terminal, forcing the other to be empty
as well; both endpoints are $x$ and both label multisets are empty.

Otherwise write the paths as $x \step{\ell_1} y_1 \reach t_1$ with labels
$\ell_1 :: L_1'$, and $x \step{\ell_2} y_2 \reach t_2$ with labels
$\ell_2 :: L_2'$.

\emph{Case $y_1 = y_2$.} By (A2), $\ell_1 = \ell_2$. By (A1) the common successor
has strictly smaller rank, so the induction hypothesis at $y_1$ gives $t_1 = t_2$
and $\ms{L_1'} = \ms{L_2'}$; prefixing the common label preserves both
conclusions.

\emph{Case $y_1 \neq y_2$.} By (A3) there is $z$ with $y_1 \step{\ell_2} z$ and
$y_2 \step{\ell_1} z$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:exists}, $z$ admits a complete
path to some terminal $t$ with labels $L$. Applying the induction hypothesis at
$y_1$ to the two complete paths $y_1 \reach t_1$ (labels $L_1'$) and
$y_1 \step{\ell_2} z \reach t$ (labels $\ell_2 :: L$) yields $t_1 = t$ and
$\ms{L_1'} = \{\ell_2\} \uplus \ms{L}$. Symmetrically at $y_2$: $t_2 = t$ and
$\ms{L_2'} = \{\ell_1\} \uplus \ms{L}$. Therefore $t_1 = t = t_2$, and
\[ \ms{\ell_1 :: L_1'} = \{\ell_1,\ell_2\} \uplus \ms{L}
   = \{\ell_2,\ell_1\} \uplus \ms{L} = \ms{\ell_2 :: L_2'}, \]
the middle equality being commutativity of multiset union---the transposition of
two labels.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
All complete evolutionary paths out of $x$ have the same length.
\end{corollary}

\begin{definition}\label{def:inv}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:exists} and Theorem~\ref{thm:jh} the following are well
defined. The \emph{normal form} $\nf(x)$ is the unique terminal object reachable
from $x$; the \emph{decomposition invariant} $\dcmp(x) \in \Mult(\Lambda)$ is the
multiset of labels of any complete evolutionary path out of $x$; and the
\emph{height} is $\ht(x) = |\dcmp(x)|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Computation from any complete path]\label{prop:compute}
If there is a complete path from $x$ to $t$ with labels $L$, then
$\dcmp(x) = \ms{L}$ and $\nf(x) = t$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[One-step law]\label{thm:onestep}
If $x \step{\ell} y$ then
$\dcmp(x) = \{\ell\} \uplus \dcmp(y)$, $\nf(x) = \nf(y)$, and
$\ht(x) = \ht(y) + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Prefix the step to a complete path out of $y$ and apply
Proposition~\ref{prop:compute}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Terminality criterion]\label{thm:term}
$x$ is terminal if and only if $\dcmp(x) = \varnothing$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) The empty path out of a terminal $x$ is complete.
($\Leftarrow$) A step out of $x$ would make $\dcmp(x)$ nonempty by
Theorem~\ref{thm:onestep}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Conservation of labels]\label{thm:cons}
If there is an evolutionary path from $x$ to $y$ with label list $L$---not
necessarily complete---then
\[ \dcmp(x) = \ms{L} \uplus \dcmp(y). \]
Consequently the label multiset of a path depends only on its endpoints: two
paths $x \to y$ carry equal label multisets, and $\ms{L} = \dcmp(x) - \dcmp(y)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on the path, using Theorem~\ref{thm:onestep} at each step. For the
consequence, cancel $\dcmp(y)$ in the cancellative commutative monoid of
multisets.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:cons} is the structural heart of the theory: $\dcmp$ is a
\emph{potential} whose differences are the path labels, so there is no
path-dependence anywhere.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:mono}
If $x \reach y$ then $\dcmp(y) \le \dcmp(x)$ (multiset containment),
$\ht(y) \le \ht(x)$, $\rk_Q(y) \le \rk_Q(x)$, and $\nf(x) = \nf(y)$. Moreover
$\ht(x) \le \rk_Q(x)$: the height is the intrinsic sharpening of the ad hoc rank
supplied with the system.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Antisymmetry]
If $x \reach y$ and $y \reach x$ then $x = y$; hence $\reach$ is a partial order.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A nonempty path $x \to y$ would give $\rk_Q(y) < \rk_Q(x)$ by (A1), contradicting
$\rk_Q(x) \le \rk_Q(y)$ from the reverse path.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Splitting and grading]
Every evolutionary path may be split at any prescribed position into two paths.
Consequently, if $x \reach y$ and $\ht(y) \le k \le \ht(x)$, there is an
intermediate stage $z$ with $x \reach z \reach y$ and $\ht(z) = k$: the
evolutionary order is \emph{graded} by the height.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Confluence]
If $x \reach y$ and $x \reach z$ then there is $w$ with $y \reach w$ and
$z \reach w$; one may take $w = \nf(x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Corollary~\ref{cor:mono}, $\nf(y) = \nf(x) = \nf(z)$, and every object reaches
its own normal form.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
A \emph{morphism of quotient systems} from $Q$ (on $\alpha,\Lambda$) to $R$ (on
$\beta,\Lambda'$) is a pair of maps $f : \alpha \to \beta$,
$g : \Lambda \to \Lambda'$ such that $x \step{\ell}_Q y$ implies
$f(x) \step{g(\ell)}_R f(y)$, and $f$ carries $Q$-terminal objects to
$R$-terminal objects.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Functoriality of the invariant]\label{thm:funct}
For a morphism $(f,g)$ and every $x$,
\[ \dcmp_R\bigl(f(x)\bigr) = g_*\bigl(\dcmp_Q(x)\bigr), \qquad
   \ht_R\bigl(f(x)\bigr) = \ht_Q(x), \]
where $g_*$ is the induced map on multisets.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A complete $Q$-path out of $x$ maps to an $R$-path out of $f(x)$ with labels
$g$-mapped and terminal endpoint; apply Proposition~\ref{prop:compute}.
\end{proof}

\section{Sharpness: the three axioms are independent}\label{sec:sharp}

To speak of chains for step relations that are \emph{not} quotient systems we use
the axiom-free notion of a \emph{chain}---a finite sequence of related
moves---and \emph{stuck}---admitting no move. For a genuine quotient system,
chains are exactly evolutionary paths and stuck is exactly terminal, so the
counterexamples really are counterexamples about evolutionary decomposition.

\begin{theorem}[Exchange is necessary]
There is a labelled step relation on $\{0,1,2\}$ with a rank function satisfying
(A1) and (A2) but not (A3), and two complete chains out of $0$ whose label lists
have \emph{different lengths} and hence different multisets.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Single label; steps $0 \to 1$, $1 \to 2$, $0 \to 2$; rank $x \mapsto 2-x$. Rank
strictly decreases and labels are trivially determined. The pair $0 \to 1$,
$0 \to 2$ cannot be completed to a diamond, since $2$ is stuck. The chains
$0 \to 1 \to 2$ (length $2$) and $0 \to 2$ (length $1$) are both complete.
\end{proof}

Without exchange, then, not even the \emph{length} of a decomposition is well
defined.

\begin{theorem}[Label determinacy is necessary]
There is a labelled step relation on $\{0,1\}$ with a rank function satisfying
(A1) and (A3) but not (A2), and two complete chains out of $0$ with different
label multisets.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Labels $\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}$; the single move $0 \to 1$ is permitted
with either label; rank $x \mapsto 1-x$. (A1) holds; (A3) holds vacuously, since
the only possible target is $1$, so the hypothesis $y_1 \neq y_2$ never applies.
The chains $0 \step{\mathrm{true}} 1$ and $0 \step{\mathrm{false}} 1$ are
complete with label multisets $\{\mathrm{true}\}$ and $\{\mathrm{false}\}$.
\end{proof}

Here the \emph{destination} is still unique; it is the labelled invariant that
fails. This isolates precisely what (A2) buys.

\begin{theorem}[Termination is necessary]
There is a labelled step relation satisfying (A2) and (A3) but not (A1) for which
no chain ever reaches a stuck object; hence there is no complete evolutionary
path and no invariant to define.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
One object with a self-loop; one label. (A2) and (A3) are trivial, and no object
is ever stuck.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Positive counterpart]
For a genuine quotient system, any two complete chains out of the same object
agree in endpoint, in label multiset, and in length.
\end{theorem}

\section{Instances}\label{sec:inst}

\subsection{The arithmetic quotient system}

Take $\alpha = \mathbb{N}$, $\Lambda = \mathbb{N}$, and declare
\[ n \step{p} m \iff p \text{ is prime},\ m > 0,\ n = pm, \]
with $\rk(n)$ the number of prime factors of $n$ counted with multiplicity.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:natqs}
This is a quotient system.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(A1): $\rk(pm) = \rk(m)+1$ for $p$ prime and $m>0$. (A2): $p_1 m = p_2 m$ with
$m>0$ gives $p_1 = p_2$ by cancellation. (A3): suppose $n = p_1 m_1 = p_2 m_2$
with $m_1 \neq m_2$. Then $p_1 \neq p_2$, else cancellation gives $m_1 = m_2$.
Now $p_2 \mid p_1 m_1$; since $p_2$ is prime and $p_2 \nmid p_1$ (distinct
primes), Euclid's lemma gives $p_2 \mid m_1$, say $m_1 = p_2 z$ with $z>0$. Then
$p_2 m_2 = p_1 p_2 z$, so $m_2 = p_1 z$, and $m_1 \step{p_2} z$,
$m_2 \step{p_1} z$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The exchange axiom in this instance \emph{is} Euclid's lemma. This is the precise
sense in which uniqueness of factorisation follows from Euclid's lemma together
with the abstract theory.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}
$n$ is terminal iff $n \le 1$; the terminal objects are $0$ and $1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Fundamental theorem of arithmetic, derived]\label{thm:fta}
If $L$ is a list of primes then $\dcmp\bigl(\prod L\bigr) = \ms{L}$.
Consequently, if $L_1$ and $L_2$ are lists of primes with
$\prod L_1 = \prod L_2$, then $\ms{L_1} = \ms{L_2}$: prime factorisation is
unique up to order.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A list of primes $[p_1,\dots,p_k]$ yields the evolutionary path
$\prod L \step{p_1} p_2\cdots p_k \step{p_2} \cdots \step{p_k} 1$, complete since
$1$ is terminal. Proposition~\ref{prop:compute} gives
$\dcmp(\prod L) = \ms{L}$, and uniqueness follows from well-definedness of
$\dcmp$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Identification of the invariant]\label{prop:ident}
For $n>0$: $\dcmp(n)$ is the multiset of prime factors of $n$;
$\ht(n) = \Omega(n)$, the number of prime factors with multiplicity; the
multiplicity of the label $p$ in $\dcmp(n)$ is the $p$-adic valuation $v_p(n)$;
and $\nf(n) = 1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Reachability is divisibility]\label{thm:reachdvd}
For $m,n>0$: $n \reach m$ if and only if $m \mid n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Each step replaces the current value by a divisor.
($\Leftarrow$) Write $n = mk$ and evolve $mk$ down to $m$ by dividing out, in
order, the primes of $k$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The deletion quotient system on finite sets}

Take $\alpha$ the finite subsets of a type $\iota$ with decidable equality,
$\Lambda = \iota$, and $S \step{a} T$ iff $a \in S$ and $T = S \setminus \{a\}$,
with $\rk(S) = |S|$.

\begin{proposition}
This is a quotient system: (A1) is $|S\setminus\{a\}| < |S|$ for $a \in S$; (A2)
holds since $S\setminus\{a\} = S\setminus\{b\}$ with $a,b \in S$ forces $a = b$;
(A3) holds because deletions of distinct elements commute.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Deletion decomposition]\label{thm:del}
The terminal objects are exactly the empty sets; $\dcmp(S)$ is the underlying
multiset of $S$; and $\ht(S) = |S|$. Hence every complete deletion sequence of
$S$ uses each element exactly once, in some order, and has length $|S|$.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{The bridge: sets of primes and squarefree numbers}

Let $\mathbb{P}$ denote the primes and, for finite $S \subseteq \mathbb{P}$, put
$\pi(S) = \prod_{p \in S} p$.

\begin{proposition}
$\pi$, together with the inclusion $\mathbb{P} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{N}$ on
labels, is a morphism of quotient systems from the deletion system on finite sets
of primes to the arithmetic system: a deletion $S \step{p} S\setminus\{p\}$ maps
to the division $\pi(S) \step{p} \pi(S\setminus\{p\})$, and $\pi(\varnothing)=1$
is terminal.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Bridge theorem]
For every finite set $S$ of primes, $\dcmp\bigl(\pi(S)\bigr) = S$; that is, the
prime factorisation of $\prod_{p\in S} p$ is exactly $S$, with multiplicity one
throughout.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:funct} applied to the morphism $\pi$, combined with
Theorem~\ref{thm:del}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
(i) $\prod_{p\in S} p$ is squarefree. (ii) $\pi$ is injective: distinct finite
sets of primes have distinct products.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
(i) By Proposition~\ref{prop:ident}, $v_q(\pi(S))$ equals the multiplicity of $q$
in $\dcmp(\pi(S)) = S$, which is at most $1$ since $S$ is a set. (ii) If
$\pi(S) = \pi(T)$ then $S = \dcmp(\pi(S)) = \dcmp(\pi(T)) = T$.
\end{proof}

Both statements are usually proved by direct multiplicative computation; here
they are transported, for free, from a trivial combinatorial fact.

\section{Universality and rigidity}\label{sec:univ}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{multiset system} on $\Lambda$ has objects $\Mult(\Lambda)$, labels
$\Lambda$, step $M \step{\ell} N$ iff $M = \{\ell\} \uplus N$, and rank $|M|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
The multiset system is a quotient system; its terminal object is $\varnothing$;
and it computes its own invariant: $\dcmp(M) = M$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof of (A3)]
If $\{\ell_1\} \uplus N_1 = \{\ell_2\} \uplus N_2$ with $N_1 \neq N_2$, then
$\ell_1 \neq \ell_2$ and there is a common part $C$ with
$N_1 = \{\ell_2\} \uplus C$ and $N_2 = \{\ell_1\} \uplus C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Universality]
For any quotient system $Q$, the pair $(\dcmp, \mathrm{id}_\Lambda)$ is a
morphism from $Q$ to the multiset system: a step $x \step{\ell} y$ maps to the
deletion $\dcmp(x) \step{\ell} \dcmp(y)$, terminal objects map to $\varnothing$,
and every evolutionary path maps to the corresponding deletion sequence of its
label multiset.
\end{theorem}

Thus multiset deletion is the universal target of the theory: every evolutionary
process is a shadow of it. Is the shadow faithful?

\begin{theorem}[Diamond counterexample]\label{thm:diamond}
There is a quotient system on $\{0,1,2,3\}$ with a single label---steps
$3 \to 1$, $3 \to 2$, $1 \to 0$, $2 \to 0$---in which the distinct stages $1$ and
$2$ are both reachable from $3$ and satisfy
$\dcmp(1) = \dcmp(2) = \{\ell\}$. Hence the universal representation is not
faithful in general.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}
A quotient system is \emph{separated} if a step is determined by its source and
its label: $x \step{\ell} y_1$ and $x \step{\ell} y_2$ imply $y_1 = y_2$.
\end{definition}

The diamond of Theorem~\ref{thm:diamond} is precisely a failure of separation.

\begin{lemma}[Pull-forward / commutation]\label{lem:pull}
Let $Q$ be separated and let $P$ be an evolutionary path from $x$ to $y$ with
label list $L$. If $\ell \in L$ and $x \step{\ell} w$, then there is a path from
$w$ to $y$ with label list $L'$ satisfying
$\{\ell\} \uplus \ms{L'} = \ms{L}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $P$, written $x \step{\ell_1} x_1 \reach y$ with labels
$\ell_1 :: L_1$. If $\ell_1 = \ell$, separation gives $x_1 = w$ and we take
$L' = L_1$. Otherwise $\ell \in L_1$; and $x_1 \neq w$, since $x_1 = w$ would
force $\ell_1 = \ell$ by (A2). Apply (A3) to $x \step{\ell_1} x_1$ and
$x \step{\ell} w$ to obtain $v$ with $x_1 \step{\ell} v$ and $w \step{\ell_1} v$.
By induction applied to the path $x_1 \reach y$ and the step $x_1 \step{\ell} v$,
there is a path $v \reach y$ with labels $L''$ and
$\{\ell\} \uplus \ms{L''} = \ms{L_1}$. Prefix $w \step{\ell_1} v$ and use
commutativity of multiset union.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Endpoint rigidity]\label{thm:endpoint}
In a separated quotient system, the endpoint of an evolutionary path is
determined by its source and its \emph{multiset} of labels: if $x \reach y$ with
labels $L_1$, $x \reach z$ with labels $L_2$, and $\ms{L_1} = \ms{L_2}$, then
$y = z$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Strong induction on $|L_1|$. If $L_1$ is empty so is $L_2$, and $y = x = z$.
Otherwise write the first path as $x \step{\ell_1} x_1 \reach y$; then
$\ell_1 \in L_2$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:pull} rewrites the second path as a path
$x_1 \reach z$ whose labels, after cancelling $\ell_1$, match those of
$x_1 \reach y$. Apply the induction hypothesis at $x_1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Faithfulness on futures]\label{thm:faithful}
In a separated system, $\dcmp$ is injective on the stages reachable from any
fixed object: if $x \reach y$, $x \reach z$ and $\dcmp(y) = \dcmp(z)$, then
$y = z$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Conservation (Theorem~\ref{thm:cons}) gives
$\dcmp(x) = \ms{L_1} \uplus \dcmp(y) = \ms{L_2} \uplus \dcmp(z)$; the hypothesis
and cancellation give $\ms{L_1} = \ms{L_2}$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:endpoint}.
\end{proof}

The arithmetic system is separated (cancellation), as is the deletion system.

\begin{theorem}[Complete divisibility invariant]
For $m,n>0$, $m \mid n$ if and only if $\dcmp(m) \le \dcmp(n)$; and if
$\dcmp(m) = \dcmp(n)$ then $m = n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Forward: divisibility is reachability (Theorem~\ref{thm:reachdvd}) and $\dcmp$ is
monotone (Corollary~\ref{cor:mono}). Backward: multiset containment says
$v_p(m) \le v_p(n)$ for all $p$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:ident}), which is
divisibility. For the second statement apply Theorem~\ref{thm:faithful} with
$x = mn$, from which both $m$ and $n$ are reachable.
\end{proof}

\section{Classification of futures}\label{sec:class}

\begin{definition}
A quotient system is \emph{saturated} if a label available one step later was
already available now: whenever $x \step{\ell} y$ and $y \step{\ell'} z$, there
exists $w$ with $x \step{\ell'} w$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Saturation is independent of (A1)--(A3)]
Consider the two-step chain $2 \step{b} 1 \step{a} 0$ with $b \ne a$ and rank
$x \mapsto x$. It is a quotient system---all diamond hypotheses are
vacuous---with $\dcmp(2) = \{a,b\}$; yet $a \in \dcmp(2)$ while no $a$-labelled
step leaves $2$. Hence availability of labels does not follow from (A1)--(A3).
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Immediate availability]\label{lem:avail}
In a saturated system, every label occurring in $\dcmp(x)$ labels some step out
of $x$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induct along a complete path out of $x$: the first label is available by
construction, and any later label is pulled back one step at a time by
saturation.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Surjectivity on futures]\label{thm:surj}
In a saturated system, every $M \le \dcmp(x)$ equals $\dcmp(y)$ for some stage
$y$ reachable from $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Strong induction on $\ht(x)$. If $M = \dcmp(x)$, take $y = x$. Otherwise there is
$\ell \in \dcmp(x)$ with $M \le \dcmp(x) \setminus \{\ell\}$; by
Lemma~\ref{lem:avail} there is a step $x \step{\ell} w$, and by
Theorem~\ref{thm:onestep} $\dcmp(w) = \dcmp(x) \setminus \{\ell\}$ and
$\ht(w) < \ht(x)$. Apply the induction hypothesis at $w$ and prepend the step.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Classification of futures]
In a separated, saturated quotient system, for every $M \le \dcmp(x)$ there is a
\emph{unique} stage $y$ with $x \reach y$ and $\dcmp(y) = M$. Equivalently,
$\dcmp$ is a bijection
\[ \{\, y : x \reach y \,\} \;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;
   \{\, M : M \le \dcmp(x) \,\}. \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Existence by Theorem~\ref{thm:surj}, uniqueness by Theorem~\ref{thm:faithful}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Complete paths are exactly the permutations of the invariant]
\label{thm:perm}
In a saturated system, a list $L$ is the label list of a complete evolutionary
path out of $x$ if and only if $\ms{L} = \dcmp(x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) Induction on $\ht(x)$. If $L$ is empty then $\dcmp(x)=\varnothing$,
so $x$ is terminal (Theorem~\ref{thm:term}) and the empty path works. If
$L = \ell :: L'$ then $\ell \in \dcmp(x)$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:avail} provides
$x \step{\ell} w$, and $\ms{L'} = \dcmp(w)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:onestep} and
cancellation; apply the induction hypothesis at $w$. ($\Rightarrow$) This is
Proposition~\ref{prop:compute}.
\end{proof}

Both the arithmetic and the deletion systems are saturated: if $n = pm$ and
$m = qk$ then $n = q(pk)$; and if $b \in S \setminus\{a\}$ then $b \in S$.

\begin{corollary}[Divisor classification]
For $n>0$ and any sub-multiset $M$ of the prime factorisation of $n$, there is a
unique divisor $m \mid n$ with $\dcmp(m) = M$. The divisors of $n$ are in
bijection with the sub-multisets of its prime factorisation; in particular, if
$n = \prod_i p_i^{e_i}$ then $n$ has $\prod_i (e_i+1)$ divisors.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Subset classification]
The stages reachable from a finite set $S$ are exactly its subsets, each
occurring once.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Factorisation chains]
For $n>0$, a list $L$ of primes is the label list of a complete factorisation
chain $n \reach 1$ if and only if $L$ is a permutation of the prime factor list
of $n$. For instance $n = 60$ admits exactly the $4!/2! = 12$ orderings of
$[2,2,3,5]$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Path integrals: weights, actions and arithmetic functions}
\label{sec:integral}

\begin{definition}
Let $M$ be a commutative monoid and $w : \Lambda \to M$. The \emph{path weight}
of $x$ is $W_w(x) = \prod_{\ell \in \dcmp(x)} w(\ell)$, the product taken over
the invariant with multiplicity. When $M$ is written additively, the same
construction is the \emph{path action} $A_w(x) = \sum_{\ell \in \dcmp(x)}
w(\ell)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[One-step law and conservation]
If $x$ is terminal then $W_w(x)=1$ (resp.\ $A_w(x)=0$). If $x \step{\ell} y$ then
$W_w(x) = w(\ell)W_w(y)$ (resp.\ $A_w(x) = w(\ell) + A_w(y)$). For \emph{any}
evolutionary path from $x$ to $y$ with labels $L$,
\[ W_w(x) = \Bigl(\prod_{\ell \in L} w(\ell)\Bigr) W_w(y), \qquad
   A_w(x) = \Bigl(\sum_{\ell \in L} w(\ell)\Bigr) + A_w(y). \]
In particular the accumulated weight of a path depends only on its endpoints.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from Theorems~\ref{thm:onestep},~\ref{thm:term} and~\ref{thm:cons}.
\end{proof}

Taking the constant weight $1$ in $(\mathbb{N},+)$ recovers the height:
$A_{\mathbf 1}(x) = \ht(x)$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:natadd}
For $m,n>0$ in the arithmetic system, $\dcmp(mn) = \dcmp(m) \uplus \dcmp(n)$.
Consequently $W_w(mn) = W_w(m)W_w(n)$, $A_w(mn) = A_w(m)+A_w(n)$, and
$W_w(p) = A_w(p) = w(p)$ for $p$ prime.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Completely multiplicative functions are exactly path weights]
Let $M$ be a commutative monoid and $g : \mathbb{N} \to M$. Then
\[ \bigl(g(1)=1 \text{ and } g(mn)=g(m)g(n) \text{ for all } m,n>0\bigr)
   \iff \bigl(g(n) = W_g(n) \text{ for all } n>0\bigr), \]
where on the right $g$ is restricted to the prime labels.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Write $n$ as the product of its prime factor list $L$; a list
induction using $g(1)=1$ and multiplicativity gives $g(n)=\prod_{p\in L}g(p)$,
which is $W_g(n)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:natadd}. ($\Leftarrow$) $g(1)=W_g(1)=1$ since
$1$ is terminal, and $g(mn)=W_g(mn)=W_g(m)W_g(n)=g(m)g(n)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Completely additive functions are exactly path actions]
Let $M$ be an abelian group and $f : \mathbb{N} \to M$. Then
$f(mn)=f(m)+f(n)$ for all $m,n>0$ if and only if $f(n)=A_f(n)$ for all $n>0$. No
normalisation hypothesis is needed: $f(1)=0$ is forced by
$f(1)=f(1\cdot 1)=f(1)+f(1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{example}
Constant weight $w \equiv 1$ gives $A_w(n) = \Omega(n)$, the height of the
arithmetic flow. The indicator weight $w(q) = [\,q=p\,]$ gives $A_w(n)=v_p(n)$,
so each $p$-adic valuation is completely additive. The weight $w(p)=-1$ gives
$W_w(n)=(-1)^{\Omega(n)}=\lambda(n)$, the Liouville function. The weight
$w(p)=p^{-s}$ gives $W_w(n)=n^{-s}$, exhibiting the Dirichlet-series kernel as a
path weight.
\end{example}

\noindent\emph{Slogan.} Completely additive arithmetic functions are precisely
the conserved potentials of the multiplicative evolutionary flow.

\section{Algorithmic content}\label{sec:algo}

\paragraph{Algorithm A (Normal form and invariant).}
Given an object $x$ and an oracle returning some step out of $x$ when one exists:
repeatedly apply a step, pushing each label onto a list, until reaching a
terminal object. Termination is guaranteed by (A1) after at most $\rk(x)$
iterations, and Theorem~\ref{thm:jh} certifies that the result is independent of
the oracle's choices. In the arithmetic instance with the ``smallest prime
factor'' oracle this is trial division, costing $O(\sqrt{n})$ arithmetic
operations per extracted factor.

\paragraph{Algorithm B (Path enumeration).}
In a saturated system, Theorem~\ref{thm:perm} says the complete paths out of $x$
are enumerated by the distinct permutations of $\dcmp(x)$: repeatedly choose a
\emph{distinct} available label and recurse. The number of complete paths is
therefore expected to be the multinomial coefficient
$|\dcmp(x)|! / \prod_\ell m_\ell!$, where $m_\ell$ is the multiplicity of
$\ell$; see Open Problem~\ref{op:census}.

\paragraph{Algorithm C (Future enumeration).}
In a separated, saturated system the reachable stages are enumerated by the
sub-multisets of $\dcmp(x)$: choose a multiplicity $0 \le k_\ell \le m_\ell$ for
each distinct label. The count is $\prod_\ell (m_\ell+1)$---in arithmetic, the
divisor function $\tau(n)$.

\paragraph{Algorithm D (Exchange closure).}
To verify (A3) for a finitely presented system, enumerate all pairs of distinct
steps out of a common source and search for a closing $z$; cost
$O(|{\to}|^2 \cdot |\alpha|)$ in the worst case.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:disc}

\subsection{What the theory explains}

The classical uniqueness theorems are not independent accidents; each is the
Decomposition Theorem instantiated at a step relation whose exchange axiom is the
subject-specific commutation lemma.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
Instance & Quotient step & Exchange axiom is & Invariant \\
\midrule
Positive integers & divide by a prime & Euclid's lemma & prime factorisation \\
Finite sets & delete an element & commuting deletions & the set itself \\
Multisets & delete an element & multiset cancellation & the multiset itself \\
Finite groups & quotient by a maximal & Zassenhaus butterfly & multiset of \\
(classically) & normal subgroup & lemma & simple factors \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The last row is the historical source of the exchange axiom's shape and the
motivating target of the abstract framework; the first three rows are developed
in full above.

\subsection{What the sharpness results tell us}

Dropping exchange destroys even the \emph{length} of decompositions---a shortcut
edge in a poset suffices. Dropping label determinacy leaves destinations unique
but labels ambiguous, showing that (A2) is exactly the axiom responsible for the
labelled refinement of the invariant. Dropping termination leaves the theory
without any complete path to speak about, which is why the rank function, though
non-canonical, cannot be omitted; it is later superseded by the canonical height
$\ht \le \rk$.

\subsection{The hierarchy of hypotheses}

\begin{itemize}
\item (A1)--(A3) $\Longrightarrow$ unique terminal object, unique label multiset,
conservation, grading, confluence, functoriality, universality into multiset
deletion.
\item $+$ separation $\Longrightarrow$ the universal representation is
\emph{faithful} on futures; endpoints are determined by label multisets.
\item $+$ saturation $\Longrightarrow$ the universal representation is
\emph{surjective} on futures; full classification of futures and of complete
paths.
\end{itemize}

Each added hypothesis is genuinely independent: separation fails in the diamond,
saturation fails in the two-step chain.

\subsection{Limitations}

The theory assumes $\mathbb{N}$-valued rank, hence decompositions of finite
length; transfinite filtrations fall outside it. The exchange axiom is a
\emph{one-step} closure condition, so systems whose diamonds close only after
several steps are not covered. Finally, the theory is qualitative: it says
nothing about the \emph{cost} of finding a step, which is where all the
difficulty lies in, for example, integer factorisation.

\section{Open problems}\label{sec:open}

\begin{problem}[Multinomial path census]\label{op:census}
In a separated, saturated quotient system with $\dcmp(x)=M$, is the number of
complete evolutionary paths out of $x$ equal to $|M|!/\prod_\ell m_\ell!$?
Theorem~\ref{thm:perm} already identifies the label lists of complete paths with
the permutations of $M$, so the question reduces to a purely combinatorial count
of lists with a prescribed multiset, with no residual dependence on the ambient
system.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Butterfly certification of composition series]
Verify that the classical composition-series setting---finite groups, steps given
by maximal normal subgroups, labels given by isomorphism classes of simple
quotients---satisfies (A1)--(A3), thereby deriving the Jordan--H\"older theorem
as an instance rather than an analogue.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Weakened exchange]
Does the Decomposition Theorem survive if (A3) is weakened to ``the diamond
closes after finitely many steps on each side, with matching label multisets''?
A positive answer would cover rewriting systems confluent but not locally so in
one step.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Euler products and Dirichlet series]
Express the Euler product / Dirichlet series formalism as a generating function
over evolutionary paths: sum $W_w$ over the future of an object and recover
$\prod_\ell (1-w(\ell))^{-1}$ in the saturated case.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Quantitative and resource-bounded versions]
Replace the qualitative rank by a cost model and ask for the cheapest complete
evolutionary path. All such paths carry the same labels, but with costs attached
to \emph{steps} rather than labels the optimisation becomes nontrivial.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Non-terminating extensions]
Develop a version with ordinal-valued rank, or a well-founded relation in place
of $\mathbb{N}$, to accommodate transfinite decompositions.
\end{problem}

\section{Conclusion}

Defining the vocabulary before attacking the conjecture paid off precisely as
intended. Once ``quotient step'' is pinned to three axioms---termination, label
determinacy, exchange---the full decomposition conjecture becomes a short
induction whose only real content is that two labels commute inside a multiset;
the sharpness of the axiom set becomes a checkable question with three
three-element answers; and the resulting invariant turns out to be functorial,
universal, and---under two further, independently necessary hypotheses---a
complete classifier of the future of an object.

Instantiating the framework at division-by-a-prime recovers the fundamental
theorem of arithmetic with Euclid's lemma appearing exactly as the exchange
axiom; instantiating at element-deletion recovers the combinatorics of finite
sets; and the morphism between them transports squarefreeness and injectivity of
the prime-product map for free. Weighting the labels turns the invariant into a
conserved potential and characterises the completely multiplicative and
completely additive arithmetic functions as exactly the path weights and path
actions of their own restrictions to the primes.

Unique decomposition, on this account, is not a family of coincidences. It is a
single fact about labelled, terminating, exchange-closed relations, wearing
different clothes.

Quotient Steps and Evolutionary Paths — numerical demonstrations.
================================================================

This is a fully self-contained, dependency-free Python program that exhibits,
concretely, every major result of the theory of quotient systems:

  A quotient system is a labelled step relation  x --l--> y  on a set of
  objects, together with a rank function rank : objects -> N, satisfying

    (A1) TERMINATION       rank(y) < rank(x) for every step x --l--> y
    (A2) LABEL DETERMINACY the label of a step is determined by its endpoints
    (A3) EXCHANGE          two distinct steps out of x close into a diamond
                           with the labels swapped

  A *quotient step* is one such move; an *evolutionary path* is a finite chain
  of them, recording the list of labels used; it is *complete* when it ends at
  a terminal object (one admitting no further step).

  DECOMPOSITION THEOREM (abstract Jordan-Holder).  Any two complete
  evolutionary paths out of the same object end at the same terminal object and
  use the same MULTISET of labels.  The resulting invariant is written
  decomp(x).

The program:

  1. implements a generic finite quotient system and checks (A1)-(A3);
  2. verifies the decomposition theorem by brute-force enumeration of ALL
     complete paths;
  3. instantiates the arithmetic system (divide by a prime) and recovers the
     fundamental theorem of arithmetic, Omega, the p-adic valuations,
     divisibility-as-reachability and the divisor classification;
  4. instantiates the deletion system on finite sets and the bridge morphism
     S |-> prod(S) between the two;
  5. exhibits the three sharpness counterexamples (one per axiom);
  6. exhibits the diamond (separation fails) and the two-step chain
     (saturation fails);
  7. verifies the multinomial path census numerically;
  8. verifies the path-weight / path-action characterisation of completely
     multiplicative and completely additive arithmetic functions.

Run with:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from itertools import combinations, permutations
from math import factorial, isqrt
from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, Hashable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Object = Hashable
Label = Hashable
Step = Tuple[Object, Label, Object]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  A generic finite quotient system
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class QuotientSystem:
    """A finite labelled step relation with a rank function.

    `objects` is the (finite) carrier, `steps` the list of triples
    (source, label, target), and `rank` the termination measure.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        objects: Sequence[Object],
        steps: Iterable[Step],
        rank: Callable[[Object], int],
    ) -> None:
        self.objects: List[Object] = list(objects)
        self.steps: List[Step] = list(steps)
        self.rank = rank
        self._out: Dict[Object, List[Tuple[Label, Object]]] = {o: [] for o in self.objects}
        for (x, l, y) in self.steps:
            self._out[x].append((l, y))

    # -- basic queries ------------------------------------------------------

    def out(self, x: Object) -> List[Tuple[Label, Object]]:
        """All quotient steps leaving `x`, as (label, target) pairs."""
        return self._out[x]

    def is_terminal(self, x: Object) -> bool:
        """`x` is terminal when no quotient step leaves it."""
        return not self._out[x]

    def has_step(self, x: Object, l: Label, y: Object) -> bool:
        return (l, y) in self._out[x]

    # -- axiom checking -----------------------------------------------------

    def check_termination(self) -> bool:
        """(A1): every step strictly decreases rank."""
        return all(self.rank(y) < self.rank(x) for (x, _, y) in self.steps)

    def check_label_determinacy(self) -> bool:
        """(A2): the label of a step is determined by its endpoints."""
        for x in self.objects:
            seen: Dict[Object, Label] = {}
            for (l, y) in self._out[x]:
                if y in seen and seen[y] != l:
                    return False
                seen[y] = l
        return True

    def check_exchange(self) -> bool:
        """(A3): distinct steps out of a common source close into a diamond."""
        for x in self.objects:
            for (l1, y1) in self._out[x]:
                for (l2, y2) in self._out[x]:
                    if y1 == y2:
                        continue
                    closes = any(
                        self.has_step(y1, l2, z) and self.has_step(y2, l1, z)
                        for z in self.objects
                    )
                    if not closes:
                        return False
        return True

    def check_axioms(self) -> Dict[str, bool]:
        return {
            "(A1) termination": self.check_termination(),
            "(A2) label determinacy": self.check_label_determinacy(),
            "(A3) exchange": self.check_exchange(),
        }

    def is_separated(self) -> bool:
        """A step is determined by its source AND its label."""
        for x in self.objects:
            seen: Dict[Label, Object] = {}
            for (l, y) in self._out[x]:
                if l in seen and seen[l] != y:
                    return False
                seen[l] = y
        return True

    def is_saturated(self) -> bool:
        """A label available one step later is already available now."""
        for x in self.objects:
            for (_, y) in self._out[x]:
                for (lp, _) in self._out[y]:
                    if not any(l2 == lp for (l2, _) in self._out[x]):
                        return False
        return True

    # -- paths --------------------------------------------------------------

    def complete_paths(self, x: Object) -> List[Tuple[Tuple[Label, ...], Object]]:
        """Every complete evolutionary path out of `x`, as (label list, endpoint)."""
        if self.is_terminal(x):
            return [((), x)]
        out: List[Tuple[Tuple[Label, ...], Object]] = []
        for (l, y) in self._out[x]:
            for (labels, end) in self.complete_paths(y):
                out.append(((l,) + labels, end))
        return out

    def reachable(self, x: Object) -> List[Object]:
        """All stages in the future of `x` (including `x` itself)."""
        seen = {x}
        frontier = [x]
        while frontier:
            u = frontier.pop()
            for (_, v) in self._out[u]:
                if v not in seen:
                    seen.add(v)
                    frontier.append(v)
        return sorted(seen, key=repr)

    # -- the invariant ------------------------------------------------------

    def decomp(self, x: Object) -> Counter:
        """The decomposition invariant: the label multiset of any complete path."""
        if self.is_terminal(x):
            return Counter()
        (l, y) = self._out[x][0]
        d = Counter(self.decomp(y))
        d[l] += 1
        return d

    def normal_form(self, x: Object) -> Object:
        while not self.is_terminal(x):
            x = self._out[x][0][1]
        return x

    def height(self, x: Object) -> int:
        return sum(self.decomp(x).values())

    # -- the theorem, checked by brute force --------------------------------

    def verify_decomposition_theorem(self) -> bool:
        """All complete paths out of each object agree in endpoint and labels."""
        for x in self.objects:
            paths = self.complete_paths(x)
            ends = {end for (_, end) in paths}
            multisets = {tuple(sorted(Counter(ls).items(), key=repr)) for (ls, _) in paths}
            if len(ends) != 1 or len(multisets) != 1:
                return False
        return True

    # -- path integrals -----------------------------------------------------

    def path_weight(self, w: Callable[[Label], float], x: Object) -> float:
        """Product of the label weight over the invariant (with multiplicity)."""
        p = 1.0
        for (l, m) in self.decomp(x).items():
            p *= w(l) ** m
        return p

    def path_action(self, w: Callable[[Label], float], x: Object) -> float:
        """Sum of the label weight over the invariant (with multiplicity)."""
        return sum(w(l) * m for (l, m) in self.decomp(x).items())


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  The arithmetic quotient system:  n --p--> m  iff  p prime, m>0, n = p*m
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = [True] * (n + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = [False, False]
    for i in range(2, isqrt(n) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            for j in range(i * i, n + 1, i):
                sieve[j] = False
    return [i for i in range(2, n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def prime_factor_list(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """The prime factors of n > 0 with multiplicity, in nondecreasing order."""
    assert n > 0
    out: List[int] = []
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            out.append(d)
            n //= d
        d += 1
    if n > 1:
        out.append(n)
    return out


def arithmetic_system(bound: int) -> QuotientSystem:
    """The multiplicative quotient system restricted to {1, ..., bound}."""
    objects = list(range(1, bound + 1))
    ps = primes_up_to(bound)
    steps: List[Step] = []
    for n in objects:
        for p in ps:
            if n % p == 0 and n // p >= 1 and n != 1:
                steps.append((n, p, n // p))
    return QuotientSystem(objects, steps, rank=lambda n: len(prime_factor_list(n)))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  The deletion quotient system on finite subsets of a ground set
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def deletion_system(ground: Sequence[Hashable]) -> QuotientSystem:
    """S --a--> S \\ {a}, over all subsets of `ground`."""
    subsets: List[FrozenSet[Hashable]] = []
    for k in range(len(ground) + 1):
        for c in combinations(ground, k):
            subsets.append(frozenset(c))
    steps: List[Step] = []
    for S in subsets:
        for a in S:
            steps.append((S, a, S - {a}))
    return QuotientSystem(subsets, steps, rank=len)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Sharpness counterexamples
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def no_exchange_system() -> QuotientSystem:
    """0 -> 1 -> 2 with the shortcut 0 -> 2.  (A1),(A2) hold; (A3) fails."""
    return QuotientSystem([0, 1, 2], [(0, "*", 1), (1, "*", 2), (0, "*", 2)],
                          rank=lambda x: 2 - x)


def no_label_determinacy_system() -> QuotientSystem:
    """The single move 0 -> 1 carrying either of two labels.  (A2) fails."""
    return QuotientSystem([0, 1], [(0, "T", 1), (0, "F", 1)], rank=lambda x: 1 - x)


def diamond_system() -> QuotientSystem:
    """3 -> {1,2} -> 0, single label.  A quotient system that is NOT separated."""
    return QuotientSystem(
        [0, 1, 2, 3],
        [(3, "*", 1), (3, "*", 2), (1, "*", 0), (2, "*", 0)],
        rank=lambda x: {0: 0, 1: 1, 2: 1, 3: 2}[x],
    )


def two_step_chain() -> QuotientSystem:
    """2 --b--> 1 --a--> 0.  A quotient system that is NOT saturated."""
    return QuotientSystem([0, 1, 2], [(2, "b", 1), (1, "a", 0)], rank=lambda x: x)

def ms(c: Counter) -> str:
    if not c:
        return "{}"
    parts = []
    for k in sorted(c, key=repr):
        parts.extend([str(k)] * c[k])
    return "{" + ", ".join(parts) + "}"


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from itertools import combinations, permutations
from math import factorial, isqrt
from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, Hashable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Object = Hashable
Label = Hashable
Step = Tuple[Object, Label, Object]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  A generic finite quotient system
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class QuotientSystem:
    """A finite labelled step relation with a rank function.

    `objects` is the (finite) carrier, `steps` the list of triples
    (source, label, target), and `rank` the termination measure.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        objects: Sequence[Object],
        steps: Iterable[Step],
        rank: Callable[[Object], int],
    ) -> None:
        self.objects: List[Object] = list(objects)
        self.steps: List[Step] = list(steps)
        self.rank = rank
        self._out: Dict[Object, List[Tuple[Label, Object]]] = {o: [] for o in self.objects}
        for (x, l, y) in self.steps:
            self._out[x].append((l, y))

    # -- basic queries ------------------------------------------------------

    def out(self, x: Object) -> List[Tuple[Label, Object]]:
        """All quotient steps leaving `x`, as (label, target) pairs."""
        return self._out[x]

    def is_terminal(self, x: Object) -> bool:
        """`x` is terminal when no quotient step leaves it."""
        return not self._out[x]

    def has_step(self, x: Object, l: Label, y: Object) -> bool:
        return (l, y) in self._out[x]

    # -- axiom checking -----------------------------------------------------

    def check_termination(self) -> bool:
        """(A1): every step strictly decreases rank."""
        return all(self.rank(y) < self.rank(x) for (x, _, y) in self.steps)

    def check_label_determinacy(self) -> bool:
        """(A2): the label of a step is determined by its endpoints."""
        for x in self.objects:
            seen: Dict[Object, Label] = {}
            for (l, y) in self._out[x]:
                if y in seen and seen[y] != l:
                    return False
                seen[y] = l
        return True

    def check_exchange(self) -> bool:
        """(A3): distinct steps out of a common source close into a diamond."""
        for x in self.objects:
            for (l1, y1) in self._out[x]:
                for (l2, y2) in self._out[x]:
                    if y1 == y2:
                        continue
                    closes = any(
                        self.has_step(y1, l2, z) and self.has_step(y2, l1, z)
                        for z in self.objects
                    )
                    if not closes:
                        return False
        return True

    def check_axioms(self) -> Dict[str, bool]:
        return {
            "(A1) termination": self.check_termination(),
            "(A2) label determinacy": self.check_label_determinacy(),
            "(A3) exchange": self.check_exchange(),
        }

    def is_separated(self) -> bool:
        """A step is determined by its source AND its label."""
        for x in self.objects:
            seen: Dict[Label, Object] = {}
            for (l, y) in self._out[x]:
                if l in seen and seen[l] != y:
                    return False
                seen[l] = y
        return True

    def is_saturated(self) -> bool:
        """A label available one step later is already available now."""
        for x in self.objects:
            for (_, y) in self._out[x]:
                for (lp, _) in self._out[y]:
                    if not any(l2 == lp for (l2, _) in self._out[x]):
                        return False
        return True

    # -- paths --------------------------------------------------------------

    def complete_paths(self, x: Object) -> List[Tuple[Tuple[Label, ...], Object]]:
        """Every complete evolutionary path out of `x`, as (label list, endpoint)."""
        if self.is_terminal(x):
            return [((), x)]
        out: List[Tuple[Tuple[Label, ...], Object]] = []
        for (l, y) in self._out[x]:
            for (labels, end) in self.complete_paths(y):
                out.append(((l,) + labels, end))
        return out

    def reachable(self, x: Object) -> List[Object]:
        """All stages in the future of `x` (including `x` itself)."""
        seen = {x}
        frontier = [x]
        while frontier:
            u = frontier.pop()
            for (_, v) in self._out[u]:
                if v not in seen:
                    seen.add(v)
                    frontier.append(v)
        return sorted(seen, key=repr)

    # -- the invariant ------------------------------------------------------

    def decomp(self, x: Object) -> Counter:
        """The decomposition invariant: the label multiset of any complete path."""
        if self.is_terminal(x):
            return Counter()
        (l, y) = self._out[x][0]
        d = Counter(self.decomp(y))
        d[l] += 1
        return d

    def normal_form(self, x: Object) -> Object:
        while not self.is_terminal(x):
            x = self._out[x][0][1]
        return x

    def height(self, x: Object) -> int:
        return sum(self.decomp(x).values())

    # -- the theorem, checked by brute force --------------------------------

    def verify_decomposition_theorem(self) -> bool:
        """All complete paths out of each object agree in endpoint and labels."""
        for x in self.objects:
            paths = self.complete_paths(x)
            ends = {end for (_, end) in paths}
            multisets = {tuple(sorted(Counter(ls).items(), key=repr)) for (ls, _) in paths}
            if len(ends) != 1 or len(multisets) != 1:
                return False
        return True

    # -- path integrals -----------------------------------------------------

    def path_weight(self, w: Callable[[Label], float], x: Object) -> float:
        """Product of the label weight over the invariant (with multiplicity)."""
        p = 1.0
        for (l, m) in self.decomp(x).items():
            p *= w(l) ** m
        return p

    def path_action(self, w: Callable[[Label], float], x: Object) -> float:
        """Sum of the label weight over the invariant (with multiplicity)."""
        return sum(w(l) * m for (l, m) in self.decomp(x).items())


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  The arithmetic quotient system:  n --p--> m  iff  p prime, m>0, n = p*m
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = [True] * (n + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = [False, False]
    for i in range(2, isqrt(n) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            for j in range(i * i, n + 1, i):
                sieve[j] = False
    return [i for i in range(2, n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def prime_factor_list(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """The prime factors of n > 0 with multiplicity, in nondecreasing order."""
    assert n > 0
    out: List[int] = []
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            out.append(d)
            n //= d
        d += 1
    if n > 1:
        out.append(n)
    return out


def arithmetic_system(bound: int) -> QuotientSystem:
    """The multiplicative quotient system restricted to {1, ..., bound}."""
    objects = list(range(1, bound + 1))
    ps = primes_up_to(bound)
    steps: List[Step] = []
    for n in objects:
        for p in ps:
            if n % p == 0 and n // p >= 1 and n != 1:
                steps.append((n, p, n // p))
    return QuotientSystem(objects, steps, rank=lambda n: len(prime_factor_list(n)))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  The deletion quotient system on finite subsets of a ground set
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def deletion_system(ground: Sequence[Hashable]) -> QuotientSystem:
    """S --a--> S \\ {a}, over all subsets of `ground`."""
    subsets: List[FrozenSet[Hashable]] = []
    for k in range(len(ground) + 1):
        for c in combinations(ground, k):
            subsets.append(frozenset(c))
    steps: List[Step] = []
    for S in subsets:
        for a in S:
            steps.append((S, a, S - {a}))
    return QuotientSystem(subsets, steps, rank=len)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Sharpness counterexamples
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def no_exchange_system() -> QuotientSystem:
    """0 -> 1 -> 2 with the shortcut 0 -> 2.  (A1),(A2) hold; (A3) fails."""
    return QuotientSystem([0, 1, 2], [(0, "*", 1), (1, "*", 2), (0, "*", 2)],
                          rank=lambda x: 2 - x)


def no_label_determinacy_system() -> QuotientSystem:
    """The single move 0 -> 1 carrying either of two labels.  (A2) fails."""
    return QuotientSystem([0, 1], [(0, "T", 1), (0, "F", 1)], rank=lambda x: 1 - x)


def diamond_system() -> QuotientSystem:
    """3 -> {1,2} -> 0, single label.  A quotient system that is NOT separated."""
    return QuotientSystem(
        [0, 1, 2, 3],
        [(3, "*", 1), (3, "*", 2), (1, "*", 0), (2, "*", 0)],
        rank=lambda x: {0: 0, 1: 1, 2: 1, 3: 2}[x],
    )


def two_step_chain() -> QuotientSystem:
    """2 --b--> 1 --a--> 0.  A quotient system that is NOT saturated."""
    return QuotientSystem([0, 1, 2], [(2, "b", 1), (1, "a", 0)], rank=lambda x: x)

def ms(c: Counter) -> str:
    if not c:
        return "{}"
    parts = []
    for k in sorted(c, key=repr):
        parts.extend([str(k)] * c[k])
    return "{" + ", ".join(parts) + "}"

    print("   weight.  Euler's totient phi is multiplicative but not completely so;")
    print("   phi(4) = 2 while the path weight of phi restricted to primes gives")

    w_phi = Q2.path_weight(lambda l: float(phi(l)), 4)

from __future__ import annotations

import random
from collections import Counter
from math import log
from typing import Callable, Dict, List

Weight = Callable[[int], float]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The arithmetic quotient system
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def prime_factor_list(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """The labels of any complete evolutionary path out of n > 0."""
    assert n > 0
    out: List[int] = []
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            out.append(d)
            n //= d
        d += 1
    if n > 1:
        out.append(n)
    return out


def decomp(n: int) -> Counter:
    """The decomposition invariant of n: its prime factorisation as a multiset."""
    return Counter(prime_factor_list(n))


def path_weight(w: Weight, n: int) -> float:
    p = 1.0
    for label, mult in decomp(n).items():
        p *= w(label) ** mult
    return p


def path_action(w: Weight, n: int) -> float:
    return sum(w(label) * mult for label, mult in decomp(n).items())


def random_route(n: int, target: int) -> List[int]:
    """A random evolutionary path from n down to a chosen divisor `target`."""
    assert n % target == 0
    remaining = Counter(prime_factor_list(n)) - Counter(prime_factor_list(target))
    labels = list(remaining.elements())
    random.shuffle(labels)
    return labels

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from typing import Callable, Hashable, List, Optional, Tuple

Object = Hashable
Label = Hashable
StepOracle = Callable[[Object], Optional[Tuple[Label, Object]]]


def extract_invariant(
    x: Object,
    pick_step: StepOracle,
    rank: Callable[[Object], int],
) -> Tuple[Counter, Object, List[Label]]:
    """Run a complete evolutionary path out of `x` and return its data.

    `pick_step(x)` must return either `None` (meaning `x` is terminal, i.e. no
    quotient step leaves it) or an arbitrary quotient step `(label, target)`
    out of `x`.  The oracle may make *any* choice at all: the Decomposition
    Theorem guarantees that the returned normal form and label multiset do not
    depend on the choices, only the returned label *order* does.

    Returns `(invariant, normal_form, label_list)` where
      * `invariant`   is the multiset of labels used (the decomposition invariant),
      * `normal_form` is the terminal object reached,
      * `label_list`  is the ordered list of labels for the particular run.

    Termination is guaranteed by the rank axiom: each step strictly decreases
    `rank`, so the loop runs at most `rank(x)` times.  A defensive assertion
    checks the axiom as we go.
    """
    labels: List[Label] = []
    cur = x
    budget = rank(x) + 1
    while True:
        move = pick_step(cur)
        if move is None:
            return Counter(labels), cur, labels
        label, nxt = move
        assert rank(nxt) < rank(cur), "rank axiom violated: the system is not terminating"
        labels.append(label)
        cur = nxt
        budget -= 1
        assert budget >= 0, "rank budget exhausted"


def height(x: Object, pick_step: StepOracle, rank: Callable[[Object], int]) -> int:
    """The common length of every complete evolutionary path out of `x`."""
    inv, _, _ = extract_invariant(x, pick_step, rank)
    return sum(inv.values())

def smallest_prime_factor(n: int) -> Optional[int]:
    if n <= 1:
        return None
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return d
        d += 1
    return n


def arithmetic_oracle(n: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Divide out the smallest prime factor; `None` at the terminal objects 0, 1."""
    p = smallest_prime_factor(n)
    return None if p is None else (p, n // p)


def omega(n: int) -> int:
    """Rank: the number of prime factors of n with multiplicity."""
    c, m, d = 0, n, 2
    while d * d <= m:
        while m % d == 0:
            c += 1
            m //= d
        d += 1
    return c + (1 if m > 1 else 0)

from typing import Dict, Hashable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Object = Hashable
Label = Hashable
Step = Tuple[Object, Label, Object]


class AxiomReport:
    """The outcome of certifying a candidate quotient system."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.termination: bool = True
        self.label_determinacy: bool = True
        self.exchange: bool = True
        self.separated: bool = True
        self.saturated: bool = True
        self.witnesses: List[str] = []

    @property
    def is_quotient_system(self) -> bool:
        return self.termination and self.label_determinacy and self.exchange

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        lines = [
            f"  (A1) termination        : {'holds' if self.termination else 'FAILS'}",
            f"  (A2) label determinacy  : {'holds' if self.label_determinacy else 'FAILS'}",
            f"  (A3) exchange           : {'holds' if self.exchange else 'FAILS'}",
            f"  => quotient system      : {self.is_quotient_system}",
            f"  separated (optional)    : {self.separated}",
            f"  saturated (optional)    : {self.saturated}",
        ]
        lines += [f"  witness: {w}" for w in self.witnesses]
        return "\n".join(lines)


def certify(
    objects: Sequence[Object],
    steps: Iterable[Step],
    rank: Dict[Object, int],
) -> AxiomReport:
    """Check the three quotient-system axioms, plus separation and saturation.

    Complexity.  Let V = |objects|, E = |steps|, and d the maximum out-degree.
    Termination is O(E); label determinacy is O(E) with a hash map per source;
    exchange is O(V * d^2 * d) = O(sum_x deg(x)^2 * d) since for each ordered
    pair of distinct steps out of a source we scan the out-neighbourhoods of the
    two targets for a common closing object.  Separation is O(E), saturation is
    O(sum over edges of (out-degree of target) * (out-degree of source)).
    """
    out: Dict[Object, List[Tuple[Label, Object]]] = {o: [] for o in objects}
    for (x, l, y) in steps:
        out[x].append((l, y))

    rep = AxiomReport()

    # (A1) termination
    for x in objects:
        for (l, y) in out[x]:
            if not rank[y] < rank[x]:
                rep.termination = False
                rep.witnesses.append(
                    f"(A1) step {x} --{l}--> {y} does not lower the rank "
                    f"({rank[x]} -> {rank[y]})")

    # (A2) label determinacy
    for x in objects:
        seen: Dict[Object, Label] = {}
        for (l, y) in out[x]:
            if y in seen and seen[y] != l:
                rep.label_determinacy = False
                rep.witnesses.append(
                    f"(A2) the step {x} -> {y} carries both {seen[y]} and {l}")
            seen[y] = l

    # (A3) exchange
    for x in objects:
        for (l1, y1) in out[x]:
            for (l2, y2) in out[x]:
                if y1 == y2:
                    continue
                targets1 = {z for (m, z) in out[y1] if m == l2}
                targets2 = {z for (m, z) in out[y2] if m == l1}
                if not (targets1 & targets2):
                    rep.exchange = False
                    rep.witnesses.append(
                        f"(A3) the diamond {x} --{l1}--> {y1}, {x} --{l2}--> {y2} "
                        f"does not close")

    # separation (a step is determined by its source and label)
    for x in objects:
        by_label: Dict[Label, Object] = {}
        for (l, y) in out[x]:
            if l in by_label and by_label[l] != y:
                rep.separated = False
                rep.witnesses.append(
                    f"separation: {x} --{l}--> both {by_label[l]} and {y}")
            by_label[l] = y

    # saturation (a label available one step later is available now)
    for x in objects:
        avail = {l for (l, _) in out[x]}
        for (_, y) in out[x]:
            for (lp, _) in out[y]:
                if lp not in avail:
                    rep.saturated = False
                    rep.witnesses.append(
                        f"saturation: label {lp} is available at {y} but not at {x}")

    return rep

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from math import factorial
from typing import Hashable, Iterator, List, Tuple

Label = Hashable


def distinct_permutations(multiset: Counter) -> Iterator[Tuple[Label, ...]]:
    """Enumerate each distinct ordering of a multiset exactly once.

    At every position we branch on the *distinct* labels still available, so no
    ordering is generated twice.  The recursion tree has exactly one leaf per
    distinct ordering, hence output-linear cost: O(k) work per emitted list of
    length k, and O(k) additional space.
    """
    remaining = Counter(multiset)
    total = sum(remaining.values())
    current: List[Label] = []

    def rec() -> Iterator[Tuple[Label, ...]]:
        if len(current) == total:
            yield tuple(current)
            return
        for label in sorted(remaining, key=repr):
            if remaining[label] == 0:
                continue
            remaining[label] -= 1
            current.append(label)
            yield from rec()
            current.pop()
            remaining[label] += 1

    yield from rec()


def multinomial(multiset: Counter) -> int:
    """|M|! / prod_l m_l! — the predicted number of complete paths."""
    total = factorial(sum(multiset.values()))
    for m in multiset.values():
        total //= factorial(m)
    return total


def complete_paths(invariant: Counter) -> List[Tuple[Label, ...]]:
    """All complete evolutionary paths out of an object with the given invariant.

    Justification.  In a *saturated* quotient system — one in which a label
    available one step later was already available now — a list L is the label
    list of a complete evolutionary path out of x if and only if the multiset of
    L equals decomp(x).  So enumerating complete paths is exactly enumerating
    the distinct orderings of the invariant, with no residual dependence on the
    ambient system.
    """
    return list(distinct_permutations(invariant))


def census(invariant: Counter) -> Tuple[int, int, bool]:
    """Return (enumerated count, multinomial prediction, agreement)."""
    enumerated = sum(1 for _ in distinct_permutations(invariant))
    predicted = multinomial(invariant)
    return enumerated, predicted, enumerated == predicted

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, Dict, Hashable, Iterator, List, Tuple

Object = Hashable
Label = Hashable


def sub_multisets(invariant: Counter) -> Iterator[Counter]:
    """Every sub-multiset of the invariant, exactly once.

    Choose an independent multiplicity 0 <= k_l <= m_l for each distinct label.
    The number of outputs is prod_l (m_l + 1); the cost is O(1) amortised work
    per output plus O(#distinct labels) to build each one.
    """
    labels = sorted(invariant, key=repr)
    ranges = [range(invariant[l] + 1) for l in labels]
    for choice in product(*ranges):
        c = Counter()
        for l, k in zip(labels, choice):
            if k:
                c[l] = k
        yield c


def enumerate_future(
    x: Object,
    invariant: Counter,
    realise: Callable[[Object, Counter], Object],
) -> Dict[Tuple[Tuple[Label, int], ...], Object]:
    """Enumerate the stages reachable from `x`, keyed by their invariants.

    Justification.  In a quotient system that is both *separated* (a step is
    determined by its source and label) and *saturated* (a label available one
    step later is already available now), the Classification of Futures theorem
    says the stages reachable from `x` are in bijection with the sub-multisets
    of decomp(x), the bijection being decomp itself.  So it suffices to walk the
    sub-multisets and materialise the corresponding stage; `realise(x, M)` is
    the instance-specific constructor of the unique stage with invariant `M`.
    """
    out: Dict[Tuple[Tuple[Label, int], ...], Object] = {}
    for M in sub_multisets(invariant):
        key = tuple(sorted(((l, m) for l, m in M.items()), key=repr))
        out[key] = realise(x, M)
    return out


def future_size(invariant: Counter) -> int:
    """prod_l (m_l + 1) — the number of stages in the future of the object."""
    n = 1
    for m in invariant.values():
        n *= m + 1
    return n

Requires: matplotlib.  Run:  python3 viz_lattice.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import random
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from math import factorial
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


N = 360  # try 60, 210, 360, 1024, 2310


def prime_factor_list(n: int) -> List[int]:
    out: List[int] = []
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            out.append(d)
            n //= d
        d += 1
    if n > 1:
        out.append(n)
    return out


def divisors(n: int) -> List[int]:
    ds = []
    i = 1
    while i * i <= n:
        if n % i == 0:
            ds.append(i)
            if i != n // i:
                ds.append(n // i)
        i += 1
    return sorted(ds)


def layout(n: int) -> Dict[int, Tuple[float, float]]:
    """Place each divisor at (x, height)."""
    rows: Dict[int, List[int]] = defaultdict(list)
    for d in divisors(n):
        rows[len(prime_factor_list(d))].append(d)
    pos: Dict[int, Tuple[float, float]] = {}
    for h, row in rows.items():
        row.sort()
        k = len(row)
        for i, d in enumerate(row):
            pos[d] = ((i + 1) / (k + 1), h)
    return pos


def random_complete_path(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """A random complete evolutionary path out of n, as the list of stages."""
    path = [n]
    cur = n
    while cur > 1:
        p = random.choice(sorted(set(prime_factor_list(cur))))
        cur //= p
        path.append(cur)
    return path


def main() -> None:
    pos = layout(N)
    inv = Counter(prime_factor_list(N))
    highlight = random_complete_path(N)
    hl_edges = set(zip(highlight, highlight[1:]))

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 7))
    fig.patch.set_facecolor("#0c1020")
    ax.set_facecolor("#0c1020")

    # edges
    for d in pos:
        for p in sorted(set(prime_factor_list(d))):
            e = d // p
            x1, y1 = pos[d]
            x2, y2 = pos[e]
            on = (d, e) in hl_edges
            ax.plot([x1, x2], [y1, y2],
                    color="#6ee7b7" if on else "#2d3a63",
                    lw=2.6 if on else 1.0,
                    zorder=3 if on else 1,
                    alpha=1.0 if on else 0.7)
            if on:

                        color="#fcd34d", fontsize=9, zorder=6,
                        family="monospace")

    # vertices
    for d, (x, y) in pos.items():
        on = d in highlight
        ax.scatter([x], [y], s=470 if on else 340,
                   c="#1f4d3f" if on else "#182247",
                   edgecolors="#6ee7b7" if on else "#3b4a72",
                   linewidths=2.2 if on else 1.2, zorder=4)
        ax.text(x, y, str(d), ha="center", va="center",
                color="#e8ecf7", fontsize=8.5, zorder=5, family="monospace")

    hmax = max(h for _, h in pos.values())
    for h in range(hmax + 1):
        ax.text(-0.045, h, f"height {h}", color="#5d6c95", fontsize=9,
                va="center", ha="right", family="sans-serif")

    npaths = factorial(sum(inv.values()))
    for m in inv.values():
        npaths //= factorial(m)
    ndiv = 1
    for m in inv.values():
        ndiv *= m + 1

    inv_str = "{" + ", ".join(
        str(p) for p in sorted(inv.elements())) + "}"
    ax.set_title(
        f"The evolutionary future of  n = {N}\n"
        f"decomp(n) = {inv_str}     height = {sum(inv.values())}     "
        f"complete paths = {npaths}     reachable stages = {ndiv}",
        color="#e8ecf7", fontsize=13, pad=18)

    ax.set_xlim(-0.16, 1.06)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.6, hmax + 0.6)
    ax.axis("off")
    fig.text(0.5, 0.025,
             "Highlighted: one complete evolutionary path. Every other maximal "
             "chain uses the same multiset of labels — only the order differs.",
             ha="center", color="#93a0c0", fontsize=10)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("evolutionary_future.png", dpi=160,
                facecolor=fig.get_facecolor())
    print("wrote evolutionary_future.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def prime_factor_list(n: int) -> List[int]:
    out: List[int] = []
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:

            n //= d
        d += 1
    if n > 1:
        out.append(n)
    return out


_paths_cache: Dict[int, int] = {1: 1}


def count_complete_paths(n: int) -> int:
    """Exhaustive count of complete evolutionary paths out of n."""
    if n in _paths_cache:
        return _paths_cache[n]
    total = 0
    for p in sorted(set(prime_factor_list(n))):
        total += count_complete_paths(n // p)
    _paths_cache[n] = total
    return total


def count_reachable(n: int) -> int:
    """Exhaustive breadth-first count of the stages reachable from n."""
    seen: Set[int] = {n}
    frontier = [n]
    while frontier:
        u = frontier.pop()
        for p in set(prime_factor_list(u)):
            v = u // p
            if v not in seen:
                seen.add(v)
                frontier.append(v)
    return len(seen)


def predictions(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    m = Counter(prime_factor_list(n))
    total = sum(m.values())
    paths = factorial(total)
    for k in m.values():
        paths //= factorial(k)
    futures = 1
    for k in m.values():
        futures *= k + 1
    return paths, futures
